# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 28 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus (ch 1-31) / P.Mich. 130 (ch 32+), Shepherd of Hermas 28 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_028_page_001.jpg

---

## Mandate 2, continued — Further on Simplicity

**1** I said to him, "Sir, I would like to ask a question." "Ask," he said. I said, "If someone in need receives but is a hypocrite, and the giver did not know this — is the giver condemned for it?" **2** He replied, "The giver who gives without knowing is innocent; but the one who received in hypocrisy will pay a penalty." **3** "The one who gives simply to whoever is in need, without making distinctions, does the right thing. The judgment falls on the deceiver. The giver has fulfilled his ministry before God." **4** "But I have heard some people say, 'I give to no one for fear of giving to a hypocrite.' What do you say to that?" He replied: **5** "All things are known to God. Therefore do not hesitate when you see someone in need — give. You are responding to what you can see; it is not for you to know what is in the heart, for only God knows that. The hypocritical recipient may deceive other people, but he cannot deceive God. He will answer for his deception. **6** The one who gives is righteous, because he has fulfilled the commandment of the Lord — to give to all who are in need. This person will be blessed and will live to God."

---

### Council Notes

Chapter 28 continues Mandate 2, developing its most practically important point through a Socratic dialogue structure. The real-world objection — "I won't give for fear of being deceived" — is exactly the kind of community concern a pastoral letter would need to address.

The Shepherd's theological resolution: God sees all hearts; the giver sees only need; therefore the giver acts on visible need and is answerable only for that visible act. The moral accounting of the heart is God's work alone.

This principle protects both the act of giving and the conscience of the giver — a liberating pastoral move. It shifts the entire ethical burden of charitable reception onto the recipient.
